reference.source: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer / NCCN genetic/familial guidelines
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline pathogenic variants in the APC tumour-suppressor gene and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, though roughly a quarter of cases arise de novo
Classic disease produces hundreds to thousands of colorectal adenomas from adolescence, with near-certain progression to colorectal cancer if the colon is left in situ
An attenuated phenotype has fewer polyps, a more proximal colonic distribution and later cancer onset

Extracolonic features include duodenal and periampullary adenomas, gastric fundic gland polyps, desmoid tumours, osteomas, thyroid cancer and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE)
Risk-reducing colectomy is planned once polyp burden is significant, with lifelong surveillance of the retained rectum or pouch and of the upper gastrointestinal tract
Desmoid tumours are a major cause of morbidity and mortality after colectomy and may be provoked by surgery
Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium and osteomas can be clinical clues that flag the syndrome before genetic confirmation
reference.pathophysiology: The condition arises from a germline loss-of-function variant in APC, a tumour-suppressor gene central to the Wnt signalling pathway. APC protein normally promotes degradation of beta-catenin, so its loss leads to beta-catenin accumulation and constitutive activation of Wnt target genes that drive crypt-cell proliferation. Somatic inactivation of the second APC allele in colonic epithelium initiates adenoma formation, and further mutations accelerate the well-described adenoma-carcinoma sequence, producing the profuse polyposis and eventual malignancy that define the disorder.
additionalInvestigations: Germline APC sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, with MUTYH testing if APC is negative
Colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy from adolescence to characterise polyp burden
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with side-viewing duodenoscopy for duodenal and periampullary surveillance
Cross-sectional imaging for suspected desmoid disease
Ophthalmological examination for congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
redFlags: Rapidly increasing polyp burden or a discrete mass suggesting malignant transformation
Symptomatic or enlarging intra-abdominal desmoid causing bowel or ureteric compromise
Duodenal or periampullary adenoma with advanced histology
Neurological features raising concern for an associated brain tumour
reference.prognosis: Untreated classic disease progresses almost inevitably to colorectal cancer, so timely risk-reducing surgery is decisive for survival. After colectomy, desmoid tumours and upper gastrointestinal malignancy become the leading causes of morbidity and mortality, making lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance essential.
pitfalls: Assuming a negative APC result excludes polyposis, when MUTYH-associated or other syndromes may be responsible
Neglecting upper gastrointestinal and duodenal surveillance after colectomy
Underestimating desmoid risk and provoking disease with unnecessary abdominal surgery
Failing to arrange cascade testing and paediatric surveillance for at-risk relatives
references: DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
NCCN Guidelines: Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment - Colorectal
management: Management centers on preventing colorectal cancer rather than treating an established malignancy, since untreated FAP progresses to colorectal cancer if the colon is left in place
Risk reducing colectomy or restorative proctocolectomy is the definitive intervention and is planned proactively before malignant transformation occurs, not reactively
After colectomy, the retained rectum or ileal pouch needs lifelong endoscopic surveillance with removal of any significant polyps
Abdominal surgery can provoke desmoid tumor formation, so surgical timing and extent should weigh this risk, and desmoids are followed with cross sectional imaging surveillance afterward

Chemoprevention with a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent such as sulindac, or a COX-2 inhibitor, can reduce adenoma burden but is used only as an adjunct to surgery and surveillance, never as a substitute for risk reducing colectomy
Upper gastrointestinal surveillance uses side viewing duodenoscopy for duodenal and periampullary adenomas, with endoscopic or surgical treatment of lesions showing advanced histology

Extracolonic surveillance also includes thyroid ultrasound for papillary thyroid carcinoma, ophthalmological exam for congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, and awareness of the Turcot syndrome brain tumor association
Flexible sigmoidoscopy screening starts at ages 10 to 12 years in known or suspected FAP, with upper endoscopy every 1 to 3 years once genetic or endoscopic confirmation is established

Genetic counseling with germline APC testing and cascade testing of at risk relatives underpins the surveillance program, with APC protein truncation testing preferred over sequencing or linkage testing
There is no staged systemic or radiotherapy pathway for FAP itself, so no drug based line of therapy sequence applies to the polyposis syndrome
If an established colorectal cancer develops, it is managed on the standard colorectal cancer staging and treatment pathway as a separate track from the polyposis syndrome
Refer to clinical genetics for germline testing and cascade screening, and to a specialist polyposis registry and multidisciplinary team for coordinated lifelong surveillance

Refer promptly for a rapidly increasing polyp burden or a discrete mass suggesting malignant transformation, a symptomatic or enlarging intra-abdominal desmoid causing bowel or ureteric compromise, an advanced histology duodenal or periampullary adenoma, or new neurological features
